info.text: Unit 10 — Interpreting a BITE readout with a colleague. CEFR B2. 23 items across Listening, Reading, Use of English and Vocabulary.

name.text: L1 · Listening · Dialogue 1 · how the fault is confirmed

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. How do the two technicians finally confirm that the fault is genuine?

generalfeedback.text: A fault is confirmed when the evidence repeats. In Dialogue 1 the CMC lists the identical fault three separate times, so the ADIRU is treated as suspect.

answer.text: The CMC lists the identical fault three times.

feedback.text: Correct — repetition in the CMC history confirms it.

answer.text: The self-test passes and the readout clears the message.

feedback.text: No — a passing self-test would give "no fault found", not confirmation.

answer.text: An ECAM warning appears for the crew on the flight deck.

feedback.text: No — the ECAM is a crew warning, not the confirmation used here.

answer.text: The connector is found loose and is then reset by hand.

feedback.text: No — that is a possible cause to check, not how they confirm the fault.

questiontext.text:
Listen to Dialogue 2 again. Decide if this is true or false:

The ground test repeats the fault code.

generalfeedback.text: The ground test runs clean and the readout says "no fault found". Because the fault appears in flight but hides on the ground, it is intermittent.

feedback.text: No — the ground test runs clean; it does not repeat the code.
Correct — the ground test is clean, which is why the fault is intermittent.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. How many separate times does the CMC list the fault today? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: The CMC lists the identical fault three separate times today, so the ADIRU is obviously suspect.

feedback.text: Correct — three times.
Listen again — the CMC lists it three times.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. On how many separate flights does the CMC show the identical code? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: The CMC shows the identical fault code on three separate flights, so FMGC 2 stays suspect even though the ground test is clean.

feedback.text: Correct — three flights.
Listen again — the history shows it on three flights.

name.text: L5 · Listening · Dialogue 3 · after the reset

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. After the reset, what does the BITE show?

generalfeedback.text: After the reset the BITE still shows 27-93, so the fault is genuine and ELAC 1 stays suspect.

feedback.text: Correct — the reset does not clear it.

answer.text: No fault found, so the message then clears.

feedback.text: No — the code stays; it is not cleared.

answer.text: A new flight-controls code for ELAC 2.

feedback.text: No — the unit named is ELAC 1, and the code does not change.

answer.text: An autoflight code for the FMGC computer.

feedback.text: No — that is Dialogue 2; here it is flight controls.

name.text: L6 · Listening · voicemail · sign as clear

questiontext.text:
Listen to the bonus voicemail again. Decide if this is true or false:

Maintenance control says you may sign the readout as clear tonight.

generalfeedback.text: Maintenance control says do not sign the readout as clear yet, because the fault is still open in the log.

feedback.text: No — the caller says do not sign it clear; the fault is still open.
Correct — the readout must stay open, not be signed clear.

questiontext.text: Listen to the bonus voicemail again. The fault code is 34-12. Which ATA chapter number does the code start with? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: The code starts with 34, the ATA chapter for navigation, so the affected system is navigation.

feedback.text: Correct — chapter 34 = navigation.
Listen again — the code is 34-12, so the chapter is 34.

questiontext.text:
Read this MEL extract, then answer.

MINIMUM EQUIPMENT LIST — ATA 34
Item: ADIRU 1 (air data / inertial reference).
Number installed: 3   Number required for dispatch: 2   Category: B
Repair-interval key: A = per remarks; B = 3 calendar days; C = 10 calendar days; D = 120 calendar days.

For how long may the aircraft be dispatched with ADIRU 1 inoperative?

generalfeedback.text: ADIRU 1 is a Category B item, and the key gives Category B a repair interval of 3 calendar days. Three units are installed and only two are required, so dispatch is allowed within that interval.

feedback.text: Correct — Category B = 3 calendar days.

answer.text: For up to 10 calendar days, as a category C item.

feedback.text: No — the item is Category B, not C.

answer.text: For 120 calendar days, because it is category D.

feedback.text: No — Category D is 120 days, but this item is Category B.

answer.text: Not at all, because two units must be working.

feedback.text: No — two are required and three are installed, so one may be inoperative.

questiontext.text:
Read this work-order extract, then decide if the statement is true or false.

WORK ORDER 55123
BITE fault code: 34-12. Self-test run: code repeated. Status: fault confirmed.

The self-test repeated the code, so the fault is confirmed.

generalfeedback.text: The work order states the self-test repeated the code and the status is "fault confirmed", so the statement matches the document.

feedback.text: Correct — a repeated code on the self-test confirms the fault.
No — the order clearly says the code repeated and the fault is confirmed.

name.text: R3 · Reading · task card · order of steps

questiontext.text:
Read this task card, then answer.

TASK CARD 34-12-00 — ADIRU 1 fault isolation
1. Read the BITE and record the code.
2. Run the self-test.
3. If the code remains, inspect the connector at the rack.
4. If the connector is clean, remove and replace ADIRU 1.
5. Run a ground test and record the result.

According to the card, what must you do before you replace the unit?

generalfeedback.text: Step 3 comes before Step 4: you inspect the connector at the rack first, and only replace ADIRU 1 if the connector is clean. You never remove a unit at random.

answer.text: Inspect the connector at the rack.

feedback.text: Correct — Step 3 comes before the replacement.

answer.text: Run a ground test and then record the result.

feedback.text: No — the ground test is Step 5, after the replacement.

answer.text: Record the code and then sign the card off.

feedback.text: No — recording the code is Step 1, not the last check before replacing.

answer.text: Replace the rack first and then the wiring.

feedback.text: No — the card does not replace the rack or the wiring.

questiontext.text:
Read this Service Bulletin header, then decide if the statement is true or false.

SERVICE BULLETIN SB-27-1043
Subject: update ELAC software to standard 4.
Compliance: recommended — not mandatory.

This Service Bulletin is mandatory and must be done at once.

generalfeedback.text: The bulletin is marked "recommended, not mandatory". Only an Airworthiness Directive (AD) is mandatory; an SB is usually advisory.

feedback.text: No — the header says recommended, not mandatory.
Correct — an SB is recommended here; only an AD is mandatory.

questiontext.text:
Read this AMM note, then answer.

AMM 22-83 — note
If the ground test runs clean, the readout shows no fault found. This does not clear an intermittent fault. If the CMC lists the code on earlier flights, keep the LRU suspect and monitor it.

Why does a clean ground test not close the case?

generalfeedback.text: A clean ground test only means the fault did not appear now. An intermittent fault comes and goes, so the CMC history still keeps the LRU suspect.

feedback.text: Correct — it comes and goes, so a clean test proves little.

answer.text: Because the self-test was not run first.

feedback.text: No — the note is about the ground test and the history, not the order.

answer.text: Because the CMC has deleted the old code.

feedback.text: No — the CMC still lists the code on earlier flights.

answer.text: Because the crew must first sign the ECAM.

feedback.text: No — the ECAM is not mentioned in this note.

name.text: U1 · Use of English · zero conditional · start

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the present tense. One word.

If the code ______ (start) with 22, the system is autoflight.

generalfeedback.text: Zero conditional: present tense in the if-clause, with third-person -s — "starts". Never will here.

feedback.text: Correct — present tense, third-person -s.
No — do not use "will" in the if-clause. Write "starts".
Almost — add the -s: "starts".

name.text: U2 · Use of English · zero conditional · pass

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the present tense. One word.

If the self-test ______ (pass), the readout shows no fault found.

generalfeedback.text: Add -es after -ss: "passes". Both clauses of the zero conditional are present tense.

feedback.text: Correct — "passes".
No — no "will" in the if-clause. Write "passes".
Almost — add -es: "passes".

name.text: U3 · Use of English · transformation · remove will

questiontext.text:
Rewrite this sentence with correct grammar.

"If the BITE will show 34, the system is navigation."

generalfeedback.text: Drop will and keep the present tense: If the BITE shows 34, the system is navigation.

answer.text: If the BITE shows 34, the system is navigation.

feedback.text: Correct — present tense, no "will".

answer.text: If the BITE shows 34 the system is navigation

feedback.text: Correct — present tense, no "will".

answer.text: If the BITE shows 34, the system is navigation

feedback.text: Correct — present tense, no "will".
No — remove "will"; write "shows".

name.text: U4 · Use of English · zero conditional · repeat

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the present tense. One word.

If the CMC ______ (repeat) the code, the fault is confirmed.

generalfeedback.text: Third-person -s on "the CMC": "repeats".

feedback.text: Correct — "repeats".
No — no "will" in the if-clause. Write "repeats".
Almost — add the -s: "repeats".

name.text: U5 · Use of English · LRU expansion

questiontext.text:
Complete the term. One word in the gap.

An LRU is a ______ replaceable unit — a box you change on the line.

generalfeedback.text: LRU = line replaceable unit. You change it quickly on the line, without a workshop.

feedback.text: Correct — line replaceable unit.
The missing word is "line".

questiontext.text: Write the specialist term that means "fit to use, and legal to fit or to fly". One word.

generalfeedback.text: The term is serviceable. Its opposite here is "not serviceable" — the unit must not be fitted or flown.

feedback.text: Correct — serviceable.
The term is "serviceable".

name.text: U7 · Use of English · negative present · do-support

questiontext.text:
Write the missing words in the present tense (negative). Two or three words.

If the reset ______ the code, we isolate the unit. (not clear)

generalfeedback.text: Use do-support in the present: does not clear (or "doesn't clear"). Not "not clears".

feedback.text: Correct — "does not clear".
Correct — "doesn't clear".
No — use do-support: "does not clear".
No — present tense in the if-clause: "does not clear".

questiontext.text: Match each term to its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: Core avionics-BITE terms: BITE (the self-check), LRU (a box you change on the line), CMC (collects fault codes), intermittent (comes and goes), serviceable (fit to use).

answer.text: the built-in self-check that stores fault codes
a box you can change quickly on the line
the computer that collects every fault code
a fault that comes and goes
fit to use, and legal to fly

questiontext.text: Match each term to its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: self-test (a unit's own internal check), readout (the message on the screen), connector (a plug to the wiring), isolate (narrow to one unit), no fault found (nothing wrong right now).

answer.text: the message shown on the screen to read
a plug that joins a unit to the wiring
to narrow the fault to one unit
the test finds nothing wrong now

questiontext.text: Match each verb to the noun it goes with on the job.

generalfeedback.text: Fixed chunks technicians use: read the BITE, run a ground test, isolate the fault, open the CMC, fit a serviceable unit.

name.text: V4 · Vocabulary · ATA chapter to system

questiontext.text: Match each ATA chapter number to the system it names.

generalfeedback.text: The fixed logic of a BITE code: 34 = navigation, 22 = autoflight, 27 = flight controls, 23 = communications.
